clinical_knowledge.topic: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes urgent initiation of therapeutic plasma exchange (PLEX) plus corticosteroids, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: fever, confusion, dark urine, and purple skin spots
Key HPI features: 42F presenting with classical pentad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, neurological deficits, renal injury, and fever. ADAMTS13 <5%.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.2C, HR 102, BP 148/92. Pallor, scattered petechiae and purpura on lower extremities, mild scleral icterus. Neurologic exam notable for intermittent confusion without focal deficits. Bloods: Hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, Platelets 12,000/uL, LDH markedly elevated at 890 U/L, undetectable haptoglobin, indirect hyperbilirubinemia. Peripheral blood smear shows numerous schistocytes. PT/PTT/fibrinogen normal (helps distinguish from DIC). Creatinine mildly elevated at 1.4 mg/dL. ADAMTS13 activity <5%, confirming the diagnosis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any neurological symptoms (confusion, seizure, weakness) — mandates urgent plasma exchange.
management_principles: Urgent initiation of therapeutic plasma exchange (PLEX) within hours of suspected diagnosis — do not delay for ADAMTS13 confirmation
Start high-dose corticosteroids (e.g., methylprednisolone 1g IV daily) concurrently with PLEX
Avoid platelet transfusion unless there is life-threatening hemorrhage, as it can worsen microthrombosis
Urgent hematology consultation; consider caplacizumab or rituximab for refractory or relapsing disease
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura TTP
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for fever, confusion, dark urine, and purple skin spots
Select appropriate laboratory studies to confirm TTP, including ADAMTS13 activity and peripheral smear for schistocytes
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: A deficiency of ADAMTS13 lets clumps of von Willebrand factor form microclots throughout the body, causing the classic pentad of hemolytic anemia, low platelets, neurological changes, kidney injury, and fever — a hematologic emergency treated with plasma exchange.
red_flags: Any neurological symptoms (confusion, seizure, weakness) — mandates urgent plasma exchange

must_ask.say: Have you had any confusion, headache, or trouble speaking?
Have you noticed any unusual bruising or purple spots on your skin?
Has your urine looked dark, like tea or cola?
How quickly did all of this come on?

history.answer: I've had a fever and felt confused over the last couple of days, and I noticed my urine turned very dark along with strange purple spots on my legs.
The fever and dark urine started about three days ago, and the confusion and purple spots showed up yesterday.
My fever has been around 38.2 degrees Celsius with shaking chills, and it has been pretty constant since it began.
I took acetaminophen yesterday, but my temperature barely came down and went right back up.
No, I have not had any cough, phlegm, sore throat, or trouble breathing.
No, I do not have any burning when I urinate, frequent urination, or flank pain.
My urine turned very dark brownish, almost like black tea or cola, starting about three days ago.
No, I have not had any abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
I have felt foggy and confused on and off since yesterday, though I don't have a severe headache or stiff neck.
I noticed tiny red dots and purple patches on my shins and ankles yesterday, even though I did not hurt myself.
No, I have not been bitten by ticks or bugs, I have no dark scabs, and my joints do not ache.
No, I have not had drenching night sweats or unexplained weight loss.
No, I have not felt any swollen glands or lumps in my neck, armpits, or groin.
No, I have not traveled out of the country recently, spent time in the woods or fields, or handled stray animals.
No one at home or work has been sick with a fever or similar symptoms.
No, I have never received chemotherapy, and I do not take steroids or any medications that weaken the immune system.
No, I do not have artificial heart valves or heart disease, and I have not had any dental procedures recently.
No, I have not started any new prescription medications or over-the-counter drugs recently.
I am in a faithful monogamous marriage, and I have never used illicit drugs or shared needles.
I have high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol, both diagnosed about three years ago.
No, I have never had any surgeries and I have never been hospitalized before.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure; I don't take any herbal remedies or dietary supplements.
No, I do not have any known allergies to medications.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink socially, maybe a single glass of wine on occasional weekends.
I work full-time as an office manager and live in an apartment with my husband.
My father had high blood pressure, but there is no family history of blood disorders, bleeding problems, or kidney disease.
My last menstrual period was two weeks ago, and my periods are always regular every twenty-eight days.
We use condoms for birth control, and there is no possibility that I am pregnant.

I thought I just caught a terrible viral bug or had a bad reaction to my blood pressure medication that's clouding my head. I'm terrified that this confusion means I'm suffering mini-strokes and won't be able to care for my kids or keep my job.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 148/92 mmHg, heart rate 102 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, body temperature 38.2°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Marked conjunctival pallor bilaterally with mild icteric discoloration of both sclerae.
Oropharynx is clear without mucosal erythema, petechiae, tonsillar exudate, or bleeding.
No cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy palpable.
Breath sounds are clear bilaterally throughout all lung fields without wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
Tachycardic rate with regular rhythm; normal S1 and S2 without audible cardiac murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender to light and deep palpation across all quadrants without guarding or rebound tenderness.
Liver edge and spleen tip are not palpable below the costal margins.
No costovertebral angle tenderness bilaterally on gentle percussion.
Multiple non-blanching petechiae and purpuric macules scattered over both lower extremities; no eschars, skin ulcers, or signs of cellulitis.
Neck is supple with full passive range of motion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Patient shows intermittent cognitive slowing and confusion regarding time, but has fluent speech and no focal motor or sensory deficits.
